title: RHCE in Cloud-native Applications
description: Prepare for EX188 and EX288 by building Shiftboard with rootless Podman, deploying it on OpenShift, and proving a release can be promoted, rejected and rolled back. Includes a portable source kit and two independent stage finals.
changelog: First public edition of the Podman and OpenShift application development pathway.

modules.title: Build and distribute a Podman image
Operate and recover a rootless two-container service
Deploy the same application into two OpenShift projects
Build from source and promote a verified digest
Package independent releases with templates, Kustomize and Helm
Verify delivery with the registry, Tekton and an installed operator

lessons.title: Start from the customer-visible contract
topics: Start from the customer-visible contract
lessons.body:
A warehouse supervisor is replacing a whiteboard. The reader needs to know who receives the next handoff and which shift owns it. A process that merely listens on a port can still return the wrong audience. In this course the release is accepted only if a second process can retrieve the expected values.

Use the **Shiftboard starter kit** reference to recover and extract the files. Read the prerequisites there. This first test runs directly on the workstation. It gives you a reference against which to compare Podman and OpenShift later. From the kit root use two terminals. In terminal A run:

```bash
mkdir -p ../board-fixture
printf '%s\n' north > ../board-fixture/audience
printf '%s\n' practice-only > ../board-fixture/token
SHIFT=morning AUDIENCE_FILE="$PWD/../board-fixture/audience" TOKEN_FILE="$PWD/../board-fixture/token" PORT=18080 python3 app/server.py
```

In terminal B run `curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:18080/report`. Expect both `"audience": "north"` and `"shift": "morning"`. The ready check returns HTTP 200. Empty only the disposable token with `: > ../board-fixture/token`. Now `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:18080/ready` returns 503 while /live still returns 200. The listener survived; a required input did not. Restore the token and change the audience to east. Predict which fields will change before refreshing /report. Restore north afterwards and stop terminal A with Ctrl-C.

The app reads the audience and token files on each request. SHIFT comes from its own process environment. Setting a different SHIFT in terminal B cannot change a running server. Save the normal and degraded status codes. These observations will help distinguish readiness, identity and data errors when several controllers are involved.

lessons.title: Choose what goes into the image
topics: Choose what goes into the image
lessons.body:
An image contains a filesystem and a default process specification. The build context is the set of local files that COPY can address. Building from the entire parent directory risks leaking test fixtures and creates accidental dependencies. Start from `app/` and read its Containerfile and .containerignore.

```bash
podman version
podman info --format '{{.Host.Security.Rootless}}'
podman pull docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim
podman image inspect docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim --format '{{.Digest}}'
podman build -t localhost/board:one -f app/Containerfile app
podman image inspect localhost/board:one --format '{{.Config.User}} {{.Config.WorkingDir}} {{.Config.Entrypoint}}'
```

The lab expects rootless true, user 1001, working directory /opt/app and a Python entry point. COPY supplies the application bytes. EXPOSE documents 8080 for tooling. The host has no mapping until a container starts with a published port. A tag such as 3.12-slim can move. Record the pulled image's digest and arch; to repeat an identical base use a FROM reference with its verified digest in a copy of the file.

Make a second Containerfile in app. Add `ARG EDITION=training` after FROM and `LABEL org.erudior.edition=$EDITION` below it. Build with `podman build --build-arg EDITION=night -t localhost/board:label -f app/Containerfile.label app` and inspect the label. EDITION was a build input. It never provided the runtime SHIFT setting. Run `podman run --rm --entrypoint id localhost/board:one -u` to confirm the effective UID. With an ENTRYPOINT, trailing run arguments go to that program; a diagnostic command may require an explicit override. Keep the original image for later lessons.

lessons.title: Deliver a pullable image and an offline copy
topics: Deliver a pullable image and an offline copy
lessons.body:
A local image ID identifies an object in one store. A teammate needs a complete registry name and permission to read the remote repository. Set REGISTRY to your lab's approved TLS registry hostname (include its port if needed), and REPO to your assigned repository path such as team-a/shiftboard. Obtain a push credential through the lab; use interactive login and the registry's trusted CA. Do not put credentials in Containerfiles, screenshots or shell arguments.

```bash
podman login "$REGISTRY"
podman tag localhost/board:one "$REGISTRY/$REPO:training"
podman push --digestfile ../board-fixture/remote.digest "$REGISTRY/$REPO:training"
DIGEST=$(cat ../board-fixture/remote.digest)
podman pull "$REGISTRY/$REPO@$DIGEST"
podman save --format oci-archive -o ../board-fixture/board.oci localhost/board:one
podman load -i ../board-fixture/board.oci
```

A push output can involve copied and reused layers. The digest identifies the transmitted manifest, not the local tag name. A later tag change does not change the bytes addressed by that digest. Test a pull by digest under a second **authorized** read-only user on a clean store. A TLS error points to endpoint name or CA trust, while denied access after the handshake points to credentials or repository scope. Correct the failing layer, then record the same remote digest on both sides.

For contrast create a throwaway container with `podman create --name board-export localhost/board:one`, export with `podman export -o ../board-fixture/container.tar board-export` and then remove just board-export. Export records the container root filesystem. It does not preserve the image layers and entrypoint as an image save/load does, or the data of external mounted volumes. Decide which artifact belongs in an offline release kit and which needs a separate backup.

lessons.title: Wire inputs to an unprivileged process
topics: Wire inputs to an unprivileged process
lessons.body:
The image is portable because its deployment supplies the shift and audience. In the kit root make the audience readable by the unprivileged app, store only dummy data, and make the credential a Podman secret. Use a fresh practice user so these names are available.

```bash
mkdir -p ../board-fixture/settings
printf '%s\n' north > ../board-fixture/settings/audience
chmod 0755 ../board-fixture/settings
chmod 0644 ../board-fixture/settings/audience
printf '%s' practice-only | podman secret create board-token -
podman run -d --name board-one -p 127.0.0.1:18080:8080 -e SHIFT=morning \
  -v "$PWD/../board-fixture/settings:/etc/board:ro,Z" \
  --secret board-token,target=/run/board/token,uid=1001,gid=1001,mode=0400 localhost/board:one
podman port board-one
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:18080/report
```

The listener uses unprivileged port 8080 inside. The host binds a different port to loopback so only local clients connect. Read-only protects content from application writes. On SELinux hosts :Z labels this dedicated bind mount for exclusive container use. Give each concurrently running independent container its own directory or use the appropriate shared-volume label for deliberately shared data. Never relabel a whole home directory.

Write south into the host audience file. When /report says south without a rebuild, you have shown that the runtime mount supplies the bytes. Show the bind target and read-only status with `podman inspect board-one --format '{{json .Mounts}}'`. Probe `podman exec board-one id -u` and `podman exec board-one sh -c 'test -s /run/board/token'`. Retain only the exit result. To change SHIFT, recreate the container with the altered environment. Stop and remove board-one before reusing its published port. Restore north in the fixture.

lessons.title: Separate the service from its observer
topics: Separate the service from its observer
lessons.body:
A pod shares a network namespace. Bind the host port once on the pod. The observer can contact the app over loopback inside that pod; an unrelated container has its own loopback. Sharing networking does not automatically give peers the same filesystem. Only the board container needs the token.

```bash
podman volume create board-audience
podman run --rm --user 0 -v board-audience:/data --entrypoint sh localhost/board:one \
  -c 'printf "%s\n" north > /data/audience; chmod 0644 /data/audience'
podman pod create --name shift-pod -p 127.0.0.1:18080:8080
podman run -d --pod shift-pod --name pod-board -e SHIFT=morning \
  -v board-audience:/etc/board:ro --secret board-token,target=/run/board/token,uid=1001,gid=1001,mode=0400 localhost/board:one
podman run --rm --pod shift-pod --entrypoint python3 localhost/board:one \
  -c 'import urllib.request; print(urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8080/report",timeout=4).read().decode())'
```

Root inside the short-lived *rootless* seeding container writes the new named volume. The actual service still runs as 1001 and mounts it read-only. If the first probe receives connection refused, inspect the server process and retry after startup. A creation dependency is distinct from application readiness. Check exact fields a second time from the workstation. Capture `podman pod ps` and `podman ps --pod` to show which container owns the business process.

Repeat with a different port for a second fresh pod and a separate named volume containing west. An untouched morning/north response from the first pod is the negative control. Stop and remove only the extra pod and its throwaway volume. Keep shift-pod through the next exercise. A named volume survives removal of its consumers until the operator explicitly deletes it.

lessons.title: Find the first failed boundary
topics: Find the first failed boundary
lessons.body:
Consider three tickets. A client gets connection refused. Another gets HTTP 503. A third gets HTTP 200 with yesterday's shift. Starting all three investigations with a rebuild erases evidence and does not change a stale environment.

```bash
podman ps -a --pod
podman port shift-pod-infra
podman logs --tail 20 pod-board
podman inspect pod-board --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}} {{.ImageName}}'
podman exec pod-board sh -c 'id -u; test -s /etc/board/audience && test -s /run/board/token'
```

Use `podman pod inspect shift-pod` to find the infra container ID if its generated name differs; run podman port on that ID. To observe lifecycle events run `podman events --filter container=pod-board` in terminal B before a controlled restart in A. Stop the events command once you capture the stop/start sequence. Compare it with the access logs of a fresh /report request. The event stream answers whether the runtime acted. The HTTP line answers whether this process received the request. Neither proves the response data.

Practice with an additional named volume whose audience file is empty. Start a separate board container with it, its own unused port, a nonempty token and SHIFT=night. Capture the 503, inspect the mount, then have the volume's writer populate that file. Compare the next /ready and /report with the earlier capture. If the port is unreachable, first locate the binding and running process. If only /ready fails, inspect inputs without disclosing secret contents. Remove these named practice resources when you have recorded your results.

lessons.title: Independent practical A — deliver a replacement workstation
topics: Independent practical A — deliver a replacement workstation
lessons.body:
A replacement workstation must serve the **night** shift for **west**. The caller connects to 127.0.0.1:18089. Your assessor will run a second client inside the same pod and later ask you to recreate the workload. Work from a clean practice user, another VM or distinct practice names, starting with the kit and registry credentials only.

Build and push the image, provide the immutable pull reference and an independently loadable image archive. Keep the audience data outside the container and use a dummy runtime secret. Supply both a recorded baseline and the commands or source needed to reproduce the stack on a fresh store. The observer must receive no secret mount. Reconfirm the same fields after replacing the service container against its saved inputs. On a separate fixture deliberately remove one required datum, demonstrate /live and /ready diverging, repair only that datum and show the restored response.

Submit the image digest, archive verification, redacted mount and port information, client outputs before and after replacement, and an incident note explaining your decisive observation. Equivalent working implementations earn the same credit. The rubric separates reproducibility, isolation, audience correctness and independent failure evidence. Production versions of this service would authenticate clients; the exercise uses a synthetic local fixture only.

```assignment
lab: local-final-evidence
```

lessons.title: Establish two project boundaries
topics: Establish two project boundaries
lessons.body:
On a workstation, an image in a user's Podman store is immediately accessible to that user. OpenShift nodes use their own runtime. A local image tag such as localhost/board:one points to each node's local environment, not your laptop. The second stage therefore builds a cluster-accessible image and deploys into two named practice projects. A Namespace scopes the resources; the same workload name can exist independently in both projects.

In your assigned disposable cluster log in using the provided developer identity and trusted API address. Set DEV and TEST to your unique assigned project names. If your lab permits project creation, create those two projects with `oc new-project "$DEV"` and `oc new-project "$TEST"`. If they already exist, switch to them. Do not use shared default or system projects for exercises.

```bash
oc whoami
oc version
oc project "$DEV"
oc auth can-i create buildconfigs.build.openshift.io -n "$DEV"
oc auth can-i create deployments.apps -n "$TEST"
oc api-resources --api-group=build.openshift.io
oc api-resources --api-group=tekton.dev
oc api-resources --api-group=cert-manager.io
```

Builds, the internal registry and Routes must work for the core release. Pipelines and cert-manager are additionally required by their named exercises. A missing API group means the cluster cannot serve that resource. A Forbidden result means the API exists but the current identity has insufficient permission. Record the exact distinction and ask the assigned lab operator to supply the missing prerequisite. Those are different repairs.

In the web console open your own DEV project, find the Workloads or Topology view and note the empty inventory. Switch to TEST and back. Compare with `oc get deployment,pod,svc -n "$DEV"`. Later you will use both the console's pod Events tab and the CLI. Write down both project names and the current API hostname before you create any resource.

lessons.title: Build inside the cluster and identify the output
topics: Build inside the cluster and identify the output
lessons.body:
In a binary build you supply the bytes when you start it. A BuildConfig describes the strategy. Starting it creates a separately named Build that records one execution. The source strategy combines an S2I builder with your files. Returning from `oc apply` only proves the API accepted a desired object.

```bash
oc project "$DEV"
chmod +x app/.s2i/bin/assemble app/.s2i/bin/run
oc apply -f build/binary.yaml
oc start-build board-bin --from-dir=app --follow --wait
oc get builds -l buildconfig=board-bin
oc get istag board:candidate -o jsonpath='{.image.metadata.name}{"\n"}'
oc tag board:candidate board:accepted
REPOSITORY=$(oc get is board -o jsonpath='{.status.dockerImageRepository}')
DIGEST=$(oc get istag board:accepted -o jsonpath='{.image.metadata.name}')
IMAGE="$REPOSITORY@$DIGEST"
printf '%s\n' "$IMAGE"
```

The base builder is fetched with an external pull specification. The output is `board:candidate` in the current project's image stream. The internal registry is the content store; ImageStreamTag tracks an image under a convenient cluster name. A Build with phase Complete plus a resolvable output digest provides stronger evidence than a build log alone. A tag snapshot into accepted represents an operator decision; you will wire that decision to a deployment later.

Open the Build details in the console and compare the source type, output and phase with `oc describe build/board-bin-1` (substitute the actual build name). If no image appears, inspect the earliest failed phase. A missing builder pull secret is different from a failure to push to the internal output repository. Confirm the cluster's image registry is healthy with the lab operator when its repository is empty, and retry the original build after correcting its input. Preserve the shell variables or reconstruct them from the stream before the next lesson.

lessons.title: Make the desired image serve real data
topics: Make the desired image serve real data
lessons.body:
The image is available, but the cluster still lacks the identity of your shift, its audience, and a runtime token. A ConfigMap separates ordinary settings from the image. The Secret carries the dummy token. A reference to either resource resolves in the pod's own namespace. Supply the inputs before starting a pod.

```bash
oc project "$DEV"
oc create configmap board-config --from-literal=shift=morning --from-literal=audience=north --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc apply -f -
printf '%s' practice-only | oc create secret generic board-token --from-file=token=/dev/stdin --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc apply -f -
oc set image --local -f deploy/base/deployment.yaml board="$IMAGE" -o yaml | oc apply -f -
oc apply -f deploy/base/service.yaml
oc rollout status deployment/shiftboard --timeout=180s
oc get svc,deploy,pods -l app=shiftboard
oc get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=shiftboard
oc port-forward service/shiftboard 18081:8080
```

Leave port-forward in its terminal. From another shell curl /report on 127.0.0.1:18081. Check both fields. The Deployment maintains replicas, the Service selects pods with app=shiftboard, and Ready controls their eligibility for ordinary traffic. Port-forward to a Service uses its selector to reach an individual pod via the API tunnel. It bypasses Service DNS and the virtual IP. To exercise that independent network path, run a new client pod in the same project after the service becomes ready:

```bash
oc -n "$DEV" run board-dns-check --restart=Never --image="$IMAGE" --command -- python3 -c 'import json,urllib.request; print(json.load(urllib.request.urlopen("http://shiftboard:8080/report",timeout=8)))'
oc -n "$DEV" wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/board-dns-check --timeout=120s
oc -n "$DEV" logs board-dns-check
```

This client must output morning/north. Use unique client names on subsequent runs; if a client fails inspect its phase and logs. The label filter on the get command finds pods; the Service and Deployment metadata in the kit carry names rather than this label. Use `oc get svc/shiftboard deployment/shiftboard` for those objects.

For external HTTPS in a routes-enabled lab, create `oc create route edge board-web --service=shiftboard --port=http`. Read the assigned host using `oc get route board-web -o jsonpath='{.spec.host}'` and request https://HOST/report using the lab's trusted ingress CA. An admitted Route is insufficient evidence without the response. Manage a reversible change in the web console: select the shiftboard Deployment in DEV, use its replica count or Edit YAML control to scale from one to two, watch both ready pods in the console, and run `oc -n "$DEV" get deploy/shiftboard -o jsonpath='{.status.availableReplicas}'`. Restore the count to one from the console. Confirm TEST was not changed. Compare the console topology and events to the actual request.

Change the ConfigMap's shift to evening with `oc patch cm board-config --type=merge -p '{"data":{"shift":"evening"}}'`. The process environment is fixed when the container starts. Predict the response before and after `oc rollout restart deployment/shiftboard`. Reconnect port-forward after the pod changes. Restore morning by the same process and verify. Mounted file projection follows different update timing from an environment snapshot.

lessons.title: Prove an image and a setting crossed the right boundary
topics: Prove an image and a setting crossed the right boundary
lessons.body:
A test project has its own service account, Secrets, ConfigMaps and Services. Possession of a digest in a handoff does not grant permission to read the corresponding project repository. For this exercise, DEV owns the image and TEST's default service account runs the pod. Use only these two assigned projects.

```bash
oc policy add-role-to-user system:image-puller "system:serviceaccount:$TEST:default" -n "$DEV"
oc -n "$TEST" create configmap board-config --from-literal=shift=night --from-literal=audience=west --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc -n "$TEST" apply -f -
printf '%s' practice-only | oc -n "$TEST" create secret generic board-token --from-file=token=/dev/stdin --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc -n "$TEST" apply -f -
oc set image --local -f deploy/base/deployment.yaml board="$IMAGE" -o yaml | oc -n "$TEST" apply -f -
oc -n "$TEST" apply -f deploy/base/service.yaml
oc -n "$TEST" rollout status deploy/shiftboard --timeout=180s
```

Issue the role-binding change with the assigned source-project administrator or have that person perform it. The grant belongs in the repository owner's project and identifies just the consumer service account. Retain the TLS checks. An already cached image can obscure whether a new pull succeeded. If you must prove registry authorization itself, use the assigned platform's audit or fresh-node pull evidence.

Now perform an independent acceptance exercise in TEST. The customer wants **night/west** while DEV remains **morning/north**. Use different local port forwards to observe individual selected pods. Repeat the in-project DNS client check from the preceding lesson separately in each namespace, using that project's expected values. Record which result came through its Service network path. Collect both responses, both project names, pod-ready evidence and each Deployment's image field. Break only the TEST workload's readiness path in its manifest, capture its pod event or probe message, then repair it; observe the rollout and final responses. A rolling strategy may keep an older ready pod serving throughout. Distinguish continuity of the old service from readiness of the new revision. Treat this as a separate scored work order.

```assignment
lab: boundaries-evidence
```

lessons.title: Build the reviewed Git revision
topics: Build the reviewed Git revision
lessons.body:
The binary build used your working tree. A controlled release must identify a commit other people can fetch. Keep the kit alone in a new repository with branch main, add the executable S2I files, and commit. Push only this synthetic source to an instructor-approved Git remote accessible to the build service. A URL accessible only from your laptop will fail before assemble begins. Use a lab-provided read credential if your remote is private.

Open build/git.yaml. Replace the example.invalid URI with your actual repository URL, keep contextDir app, and set ref to the SHA you intend to build for a reproducible manual build. For a branch-driven webhook exercise use the assigned branch and record the resolved Build revision instead. Do not commit personal tokens or a generated webhook URL. Back in DEV, create the webhook Secret containing a random disposable value under the exact key WebHookSecretKey. A pipeline-friendly way to supply it is:

```bash
python3 -c 'import secrets,sys;sys.stdout.write(secrets.token_hex(24))' | oc -n "$DEV" create secret generic board-hook --from-file=WebHookSecretKey=/dev/stdin
oc -n "$DEV" apply -f build/git.yaml
oc -n "$DEV" start-build board-git --follow --wait
oc -n "$DEV" get builds -l buildconfig=board-git
```

For the resulting build name, read `oc -n "$DEV" get build/NAME -o jsonpath='{.spec.revision.git.commit}{" "}{.status.phase}{"\n"}'`. Compare with the exact source commit. The image stream should now point to a candidate produced by this named Build.

Inspect app/.s2i/bin/assemble and run. The wrapper calls this builder's stock /usr/libexec/s2i/assemble before checking Python syntax under /opt/app-root/src. The run override uses exec so the HTTP server receives container signals. For another builder, consult its documented paths and runtime contract. Customize an additional syntactic or version check in the wrapper on your practice branch. Demonstrate that the executing build log and commit actually correspond to your revision.

lessons.title: Package a reusable source-validation builder
topics: Package a reusable source-validation builder
lessons.body:
Two teams can copy an assemble hook, but sharing a named builder lets you version the validator and its interpreter together. A custom *S2I builder image* still uses the source strategy. OpenShift's separately named Custom build strategy is a different mechanism and is unnecessary for this exercise.

Read builder/Containerfile. It derives from the same UBI Python builder, retaining its S2I metadata, and copies a short source-validation program to /usr/local/bin. The script stays executable in the image only if its executable mode is preserved in the build context. In DEV, make a binary Docker-strategy builder that consumes this directory, then use its resulting image stream tag from a second Source BuildConfig.

```bash
chmod +x builder/validate-source
cp builder/Containerfile builder/Dockerfile
oc -n "$DEV" new-build --name=board-builder --binary --strategy=docker
oc -n "$DEV" start-build board-builder --from-dir=builder --follow --wait
oc -n "$DEV" get istag board-builder:latest -o jsonpath='{.image.metadata.name}{"\n"}'
```

In a working copy of build/binary.yaml keep the existing board ImageStream, rename the BuildConfig board-checked, set its sourceStrategy.from to `{kind: ImageStreamTag, name: 'board-builder:latest'}`, and change the output tag to board:checked. Copy app into a separate working directory, preserve its executable files and add `/usr/local/bin/board-validate-source /opt/app-root/src/server.py` after the stock assemble step. Submit the modified build config, then start board-checked with that copied application directory. Record the exact builder and result digests. The build pod first pulls the derived builder; the source wrapper then invokes its additional tool.

For feedback, spell the tool's path incorrectly in the working copy, start a separate run and find its failed phase. Correct the reference and repeat, then verify /report on a small deployment from the checked image. The sequence distinguishes the builder actually used, a source failure after the builder was acquired, and the health of the delivered application. Do not promote an image solely because the builder itself built successfully.

lessons.title: Make a bad candidate fail before promotion
topics: Make a bad candidate fail before promotion
lessons.body:
A source commit, an artifact build and a production rollout are three different events. A webhook starts a build. A postCommit hook tests the freshly built image before it can be pushed. A workload image-change trigger updates a pod template. Confusing these boundaries can deploy a candidate that has only passed compilation.

The kit's Git BuildConfig runs the supplied checks/image-contract.py script in the output image. It imports the built source and checks that Handler.do_GET is callable. The hook uses a temporary container. A successful test does not modify the delivered filesystem. In DEV record the current board:candidate and board:accepted digests. Create a copy of the Git BuildConfig with a unique metadata.name, no triggers, output board:rejected-test, and a deliberately failing hook `command: ["python3", "-c", "raise SystemExit(7)"]`. Use your real source URL and revision. Start that named build and inspect its status, log and events. The checker should fail, the rejected output tag should not be newly published and accepted should retain its prior digest. Restore the valid check and use a new output tag for a positive control.

Inspect the generic trigger already defined in board-git. In the approved lab, have the assigned Git server or instructor-configured webhook sender post a generic event to the private webhook URL shown by `oc describe bc/board-git`. The URL's secret and any credentials stay out of screenshots. Some clusters restrict unauthenticated webhook endpoints. Use the lab's supported authenticated integration and ask its operator about webhook permissions if the request is denied. Compare the new Build's trigger cause and resolved source SHA with your manual run. Changing a file locally without pushing it is a useful negative control.

Release choice: accept a candidate by digest after the customer endpoint has passed. Preserve the earlier accepted digest for rollback. A failed build and a rejected healthy build are distinct outcomes; your record should identify which one occurred.

lessons.title: Promote and roll back an image without rebuilding it
topics: Promote and roll back an image without rebuilding it
lessons.body:
Use one build output and move its tag through an explicit acceptance decision. Board:accepted is in the DEV project; attach its image-change trigger only to the board container of the DEV Deployment. A Kubernetes Deployment does not automatically watch OpenShift image streams merely because a tag appears in its image field.

```bash
oc project "$DEV"
oc set triggers deploy/shiftboard --from-image=board:accepted -c board
oc get deploy/shiftboard -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.image\.openshift\.io/triggers}{"\n"}'
PREVIOUS=$(oc get istag board:accepted -o jsonpath='{.image.metadata.name}')
CANDIDATE=$(oc get istag board:candidate -o jsonpath='{.image.metadata.name}')
oc tag "board@$CANDIDATE" board:accepted
oc rollout status deploy/shiftboard --timeout=180s
oc get deploy/shiftboard -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
```

Use distinct real image contents to practice a rollout. A candidate equal to the accepted digest can validly cause no rollout. For example, add a reviewed `/version` response in a new Git commit, run the build and test that specific path on a small candidate deployment before promotion. Observe the workload image change before trusting rollout status, which can briefly report success for the previous template. Check the target container's image field, the new available revision, and the client response. Runtime imageID may use a transport-specific representation; distinguish it from the pullable manifest reference.

Your independent release work order is to admit the new version in DEV, leave TEST on its known digest, then restore the old DEV version using `oc tag "board@$PREVIOUS" board:accepted`. Capture both expected application responses and unchanged TEST. Retagging with the former digest reuses a previously validated artifact. Rebuilding from a branch named yesterday would produce a different chain of evidence. Keep the old image available in the stream during the exercise.

```assignment
lab: promotion-evidence
```

lessons.title: Parameterize two cooperating containers
topics: Parameterize two cooperating containers
lessons.body:
A supervisor wants a second copy with an observer that checks readiness and logs the numeric result. A reusable OpenShift Template gives users a small parameter interface. In templates/board.yaml, NAME feeds resource names, selectors and config references. The board container receives the Secret mount. The observer receives neither the Secret nor the audience mount. It uses the pod network to query localhost and logs only a short health result.

```bash
oc project "$DEV"
oc process --parameters -f templates/board.yaml
oc process -f templates/board.yaml -p NAME=paired -p IMAGE="$IMAGE" -p SHIFT=late -p AUDIENCE=outbound > ../board-fixture/paired.yaml
oc apply --dry-run=server -f ../board-fixture/paired.yaml
oc apply -f ../board-fixture/paired.yaml
oc rollout status deploy/paired --timeout=180s
oc logs deploy/paired -c observer --tail=8
oc port-forward svc/paired 18084:8080
```

From another terminal read /report and compare it with the ordinary DEV shiftboard. Seeing the observer log ready 200 proves a pod-local check. The forwarded response checks the selected pod via the API tunnel. To test actual Service discovery and forwarding, run the independent client-pod command from the deployment lesson with a fresh client name and URL http://paired:8080/report. Its separate pod must return late/outbound. A script using `oc logs` without a container name can show the wrong process. Select -c board and -c observer deliberately.

For guided customization add a new template parameter for the observer delay. Route it through an environment variable into the observer container, parse it as an integer in Python, and set a bounded positive value. Process a fresh template into a distinct name, inspect the generated YAML, and time two consecutive log entries. Return to the default without disturbing the original release. A missing required IMAGE should make processing fail before resources are deployed.

lessons.title: Use a Kustomize overlay without changing the base
topics: Use a Kustomize overlay without changing the base
lessons.body:
The base describes a program and its port. An evening environment needs two replicas and different settings. Kustomize transforms the resources before the API sees them. It can create content-hashed ConfigMap names and rewrite recognized references, so a settings change changes the pod template instead of waiting for stale process environments.

Work in TEST only. Copy the whole deploy directory into a fresh temporary workspace to preserve the original. In the evening kustomization change newName to the actual source image repository and replace newTag with `digest: sha256:...` using the accepted digest from DEV. The source environment must allow the TEST service account to pull it as in the earlier handoff. No placeholder REPLACE_PROJECT should remain.

```bash
oc kustomize deploy/overlays/evening > ../board-fixture/evening-rendered.yaml
oc -n "$TEST" apply --dry-run=server -f ../board-fixture/evening-rendered.yaml
oc -n "$TEST" apply -f ../board-fixture/evening-rendered.yaml
oc -n "$TEST" rollout status deploy/shiftboard --timeout=180s
oc -n "$TEST" get deployment/shiftboard -o jsonpath='{.status.availableReplicas}{"\n"}'
```

Run from the working copy. Inspect the rendered name in both the ConfigMap and Deployment before applying. Both must contain the same generated suffix. The expected test response is evening/south, with two available replicas. Change only the audience literal in the working overlay to east, render a second file and compare resource names and pod template references. A changed reference should cause a new rollout. Keep the installed Secret separate. Persist the accepted source and inspect the earlier name before deciding whether an old ConfigMap is still referenced. The forward from a previous pod may need to be reopened.

lessons.title: Use Helm to upgrade and reverse a customer release
topics: Use Helm to upgrade and reverse a customer release
lessons.body:
A chart distributes templates with a values interface. A Helm release records the resulting objects and revisions. When the same chart is instantiated twice, resource names and selectors must not collide. The kit uses the release name for the Service, Deployment and private ConfigMap. The token comes from an existing Secret. The chart requires an explicit pullable image.

```bash
helm lint chart --set-string image="$IMAGE"
helm template trial chart --set-string image="$IMAGE" > ../board-fixture/chart-rendered.yaml
helm upgrade --install trial chart -n "$TEST" --set-string image="$IMAGE" --set-string shift=morning --set-string audience=bay --wait --timeout 3m
helm history trial -n "$TEST"
oc -n "$TEST" port-forward svc/trial 18085:8080
```

Read /report from another terminal. Then upgrade with the original image and values, changing audience to dock. The ConfigMap alone could change without replacing an environment-based process. Read the chart's pod-template checksum annotation: a change to either setting changes that template. Check the new available revision and returned bytes. Capture the previous revision number from history, run `helm rollback trial REVISION -n "$TEST" --wait --timeout 3m`, then reconnect and prove that bay is back. Rollback creates a new revision containing earlier desired state.

For a multi-container chart release, set observer=true in the release values. The extra container polls the shared pod loopback and logs a status without mounting the credential. Check both names in the rendered pod spec and use oc logs -c observer for the installed release. Next author a small chart of your own in an empty directory. Give it a Chart.yaml with apiVersion v2, a chart name and version; write values.yaml with an audience string, and add a templates/receipt.yaml ConfigMap whose metadata.name is `{{ .Release.Name }}-receipt` and whose data.audience uses `{{ .Values.audience | quote }}`. Do not copy the supplied application's templates for this task. Render it twice under two release names and two values. Install both practice releases in TEST and read both ConfigMaps by name. Upgrade the first with a different audience while the second stays unchanged. This exercises the division between chart metadata, a parameter value and an individual release. Deliver the new chart source and both observed receipts.

For the packaging handoff, create a separate two-container release from the Template and a two-replica overlay on TEST. Deliver a values file for a third distinct chart release, upgrade and roll it back. Show proof that one release's changed audience did not affect the others. Check whether a server-side resource rejection, render error or application mismatch first explains a deliberately invalid parameter. Submit the render and the independently read outputs.

```assignment
lab: chart-evidence
```

lessons.title: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
topics: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
lessons.body:
Inside the cluster, builds can push to the image-registry Service and workloads can pull by their service-account identity. A developer laptop cannot generally resolve the internal service DNS name. Trying the same address on both sides confuses name resolution, network reachability, TLS and authorization. Begin with `oc -n "$DEV" get is board -o jsonpath='{.status.dockerImageRepository}{"\n"}'` and compare that address to the approved external registry endpoint supplied for this lab.

On a dedicated cluster where you are explicitly the platform administrator for this exercise, inspect `oc get configs.imageregistry.operator.openshift.io/cluster -o yaml` and record spec.defaultRoute and the observed Available condition. If registry storage and ingress are ready and the lab design calls for the operator-managed external route, set `oc patch configs.imageregistry.operator.openshift.io/cluster --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"defaultRoute":true}}'`. Wait for the default-route in openshift-image-registry to be admitted. Identify its host, and configure your workstation to trust its issuer through your lab's documented CA process. Restore the prior unset/false/true value when finished. For a shared developer sandbox, use the endpoint or internal-only workflow supplied by its operator.

With a reachable approved external registry, log in as the authorized project developer using a temporary auth file. Avoid expanding a token into a command argument or a lab submission.

```bash
authdir=$(mktemp -d)
oc whoami -t | podman login --authfile "$authdir/auth.json" --username "$(oc whoami)" --password-stdin "$REGISTRY_HOST"
podman pull --authfile "$authdir/auth.json" "$REGISTRY_HOST/$DEV/board@$DIGEST"
podman logout --authfile "$authdir/auth.json" "$REGISTRY_HOST"
rm -f "$authdir/auth.json"
rmdir "$authdir"
```

Use the actual admitted route host for REGISTRY_HOST. Compare the pulled image with the stream digest and record the namespace, identity and issuer, never the login token. A valid TLS handshake followed by a repository access error points you toward project scope. Turning off certificate verification would discard evidence at the wrong boundary.

lessons.title: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
topics: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
lessons.body:
A successful build does not ask the deployed service which shift is on duty. A Tekton Task can express that check. A Pipeline references the Task and binds its parameters. A PipelineRun captures the inputs and results for one invocation. Each run is evidence about one endpoint at a particular time. Reusing its old success after a deployment change is a grading error.

Open pipeline/verify.yaml. The Task receives endpoint and expectedShift through environment variables rather than interpolating untrusted text into executable script. The step treats a connection problem, non-2xx response, invalid JSON and wrong field as failures. In DEV make sure service/shiftboard is ready with shift=morning. Projects isolate short service names so the PipelineRun must execute in that same project.

```bash
oc -n "$DEV" apply -f pipeline/verify.yaml
RUN=$(oc -n "$DEV" create -f pipeline/run.yaml -o name)
oc -n "$DEV" get "$RUN" -w
```

Stop the watch after the run finishes. Read `oc -n "$DEV" get "$RUN" -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Succeeded")].status}{"\n"}'`. Expect True. List TaskRuns with the label tekton.dev/pipelineRun=RUN_NAME, then find the pod using tekton.dev/taskRun=TASKRUN_NAME. Read the step-check logs. A pending pod that cannot pull the Python image has not tested the application.

Now create a second copy of run.yaml with expectedShift=obsolete. Submit it with oc create so generateName gives a new run, and confirm Succeeded=False with a specific shift mismatch. Fix only the expectation and create a third run. For the scored workflow assignment, add a second named Task that checks audience=north, then wire that task after acceptance using runAfter. Capture the skipped/downstream state for a failing first step and both successes on a fresh positive run. Keep the original failed result as part of your handoff.

```assignment
lab: pipeline-evidence
```

lessons.title: Consume an installed operator through its API
topics: Consume an installed operator through its API
lessons.body:
An operator adds a control loop for a product-specific resource. A developer writes an instance of a supported custom kind and checks the status produced by its controller. A CRD served by the API tells you which shapes are allowed. It does not guarantee the controller is running, the current identity can create an instance, or the required backing resources exist.

Assume the lab operator installed cert-manager and allows a namespaced self-signed practice issuer. Examine the resource schema, permissions and namespaced instance first. These resources are confined to the chosen developer project.

```bash
oc api-resources --api-group=cert-manager.io
oc -n "$DEV" auth can-i create certificates.cert-manager.io
oc explain certificate.spec.issuerRef
oc -n "$DEV" apply -f operator/certificate.yaml
oc -n "$DEV" wait --for=condition=Ready issuer/board-practice --timeout=120s
oc -n "$DEV" wait --for=condition=Ready certificate/board-certificate --timeout=120s
oc -n "$DEV" get secret board-local-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}{"\n"}'
```

The Certificate names a controller-managed Secret. Check that its type is kubernetes.io/tls and display only the **public certificate** subject and SAN if you need to inspect it: `oc -n "$DEV" get secret board-local-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName`. The DNS entry should include shiftboard. Avoid printing the entire Secret. A self-signed fixture is for controller practice, not a public trust chain.

For a fault exercise, create a second Certificate with unique metadata.name and secretName and a nonexistent namespaced issuerRef. Find the first resource condition or CertificateRequest event that explains the pending request. Repair the reference, watch a fresh Ready condition and verify the second Secret's type and public SAN. The original Certificate should stay Ready throughout. If the lab lacks the operator, render the objects and record the missing API, then run the live exercise on the designated equipped cluster before marking this practical complete.

```assignment
lab: operator-evidence
```

lessons.title: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
topics: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
lessons.body:
A distribution center asks for a reviewed release that can be rebuilt from Git and accepted without guessing which image is running. The developer's service in the source project must serve **day/receiving**. An independently configured two-replica service in a second project must serve **night/shipping**. Use fresh resource names or two reset disposable projects. Start from the kit and a fresh approved commit. Provision the workloads with a packaging method another developer can repeat. Keep private runtime values out of application and build logs.

Implement a meaningful new version marker at /version. Deliver a BuildConfig, a Git source revision, a passing build-time check and evidence of a separate rejected build. Publish a candidate to the internal registry and promote a selected digest to the source workload. A test-side two-container release must include a read-only observer that receives no token. Keep evidence of both projects' independent behavior. Have a second developer or clean checkout reconcile a fresh service in the target project from the submitted source.

Run a passing Tekton acceptance check, then generate one intentionally failing run by changing only the expected shift and a passing replacement run. Create a namespaced Certificate using the installed operator and inspect the public outcome. Finally withdraw the new release from the source workload by restoring a prior accepted digest. Prove the version response changed as planned while the target project still returns its required data. If using two identical images, you have not yet demonstrated rollback. Prepare an older baseline first.

Submit exact source commit, Build and PipelineRun identities, digest references, rendered manifests, selected status conditions, two endpoint readings and a short rollback note. An observer should be able to reproduce the result without your shell history or any real credential. A green CI status and a page screenshot by themselves cannot establish image provenance, application data and isolation.

```assignment
lab: cluster-final-evidence
```

questions.stem: Which two behaviors should you verify after a Helm rollback?
choices: The selected earlier business values are visible at the endpoint
The original container UID must change
The chart source directory disappears
The release history records a new rollback revision
questions.explanation: Historical desired state is reapplied, and the rollback itself becomes a revision.

questions.topic: Use Helm to upgrade and reverse a customer release
questions.stem: Which annotation key does the supplied chart set on its pod template to trigger a rollout after application settings change?
questions.explanation: The chart writes this checksum annotation on spec.template.metadata.annotations so a settings change alters the pod template.

questions.topic: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
questions.stem: A laptop cannot resolve a cluster Service DNS name but the workload inside can pull. What is the next action for the developer?
choices: Disable TLS verification
Find the approved external registry route or use the internal workflow
Delete the image stream
questions.explanation: An in-cluster DNS name is typically unsuitable as a laptop endpoint.

questions.topic: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
questions.stem: Which two pieces of information can be kept in a non-secret registry handoff?
choices: The access token
The authorization header
The verified repository digest
The approved registry hostname
questions.explanation: Digest and hostname identify the deliverable. Authentication material must remain private.

questions.topic: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
questions.stem: Who should change spec.defaultRoute on the registry operator configuration for this exercise?
choices: Any user who can read a project
Every developer on first login
The explicitly assigned platform administrator of the dedicated lab
questions.explanation: The setting is cluster-wide and requires platform-level coordination.

questions.topic: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
questions.stem: Match a Tekton resource with the responsibility in this exercise.
choices: One invocation and its status
A repeatable group of executable steps
Ordering and wiring reusable work
questions.explanation: A success belongs to one PipelineRun and its inputs.

questions.topic: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
questions.stem: A PipelineRun stays pending while its step image cannot be pulled. What does it establish about the customer endpoint?
choices: The endpoint returned 500
The acceptance probe has not executed
The expected shift is correct
questions.explanation: The step must execute before it can make any observation about the application.

questions.topic: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
questions.stem: What is the name of the condition type checked on the completed PipelineRun to distinguish pass from fail?
questions.explanation: Read that condition’s status on the specific PipelineRun.

questions.topic: Consume an installed operator through its API
questions.stem: The Certificate API is served, but a new Certificate references a nonexistent Issuer. What evidence best locates the dependency failure?
choices: A local image tag
A sibling Service port
This Certificate’s conditions and its CertificateRequest events
questions.explanation: The resource can be accepted while the controller waits for its named issuer.

questions.topic: Consume an installed operator through its API
questions.stem: Which evidence can confirm the delivered certificate without disclosing its private key?
choices: Read only the public certificate SAN
Dump tls.key to the submission
Inspect Ready and the Secret type
Export every Secret in the project
questions.explanation: Controller status plus the public certificate/type can establish the required outcome without exposing private material.

questions.topic: Consume an installed operator through its API
questions.stem: Which Secret type should cert-manager produce in the exercise?
questions.explanation: This is the Kubernetes TLS Secret type. The private key remains in the Secret.

questions.topic: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
questions.stem: Which two independent records establish a promotion from reviewed Git to the actual customer workload?
choices: The Build’s resolved source commit and resulting digest
A screenshot of a green home page alone
The deployed image reference and distinct version response
The local date of the diagram
questions.explanation: Provenance and customer-visible behavior answer different parts of the release claim.

questions.topic: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
questions.stem: A deliberately failing PipelineRun is followed by a corrected run. What should the handoff preserve?
choices: Only a screenshot of the successful page
Both run identities, their inputs and observed conditions
Only the Pipeline definition
questions.explanation: The two outcomes show the check discriminated between valid and invalid expectations.

questions.topic: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
questions.stem: What is the clearest negative control for a source-only rollback across two projects?
choices: The target project still returns its intended data and retains its assigned image
The local shell still contains IMAGE
An old BuildConfig still exists
questions.explanation: The target is deliberately excluded from the rollback, so observe its actual state and business data.

decks.title: Build and distribute a Podman image

cards.topic: Start from the customer-visible contract
cards.front: Why is /report a stronger release check than a listening port?
cards.back: It reads the configuration and returns the exact customer-visible data through the application.

cards.topic: Start from the customer-visible contract
cards.front: When would /live pass on a configuration incident?
cards.back: The HTTP handler can answer while a required setting is empty or unreadable, so /ready can fail.

cards.topic: Choose what goes into the image
cards.front: How does the build context affect reproducibility and disclosure?
cards.back: It bounds available COPY sources. Keep fixtures, credentials and unrelated parent directories outside it.

cards.topic: Choose what goes into the image
cards.front: What does a digest give you that a mutable base tag does not?
cards.back: A content-addressed identity for a particular manifest. Record architecture and the pull reference as well.

cards.topic: Deliver a pullable image and an offline copy
cards.front: Why save an image and back up a mounted volume separately?
cards.back: The image archive preserves layers and metadata. An external volume has an independent lifetime and contents.

cards.topic: Deliver a pullable image and an offline copy
cards.front: What evidence distinguishes a registry trust issue from repository permission?
cards.back: A certificate or name error occurs during TLS. A repository denial after a valid handshake points toward authentication or scope.

decks.title: Operate and recover a rootless two-container service

cards.topic: Wire inputs to an unprivileged process
cards.front: What does the host-side 127.0.0.1 in a port mapping control?
cards.back: It restricts the host listener to loopback. The container can still listen on its own interfaces.

cards.topic: Wire inputs to an unprivileged process
cards.front: How can you prove a credential is mounted without recording it?
cards.back: Check the expected file is readable and nonempty as the service UID, then observe application behavior.

cards.topic: Separate the service from its observer
cards.front: How can the observer reach the service without receiving its data mounts?
cards.back: It shares the pod network namespace and requests loopback HTTP. Each container has its own mount list.

cards.topic: Separate the service from its observer
cards.front: How do you distinguish named-volume survival from a newly seeded equivalent?
cards.back: Record the volume identity and a unique test value, replace the consumer without reseeding, then reread it.

cards.topic: Find the first failed boundary
cards.front: Which observation distinguishes a reachable but misconfigured app from a missing listener?
cards.back: An HTTP response such as 503 proves a handler replied. Connection refusal occurs before an HTTP response.

cards.topic: Find the first failed boundary
cards.front: Which observations answer when a container restarted and which request it saw?
cards.back: Use runtime events for the lifecycle and application logs for requests.

cards.topic: Independent practical A — deliver a replacement workstation
cards.front: Which evidence should accompany a portable delivery digest?
cards.back: The registry/repository, fresh pull or archive load, startup inputs and a verified customer response.

cards.topic: Independent practical A — deliver a replacement workstation
cards.front: What should a replacement test avoid reusing as its only proof?
cards.back: The original running container. Recreate the service and read the required result independently.

decks.title: Deploy the same application into two OpenShift projects

cards.topic: Establish two project boundaries
cards.front: Why test discovery and authorization separately?
cards.back: The API must serve the resource kind, and the active identity must have permission in the target project.

cards.topic: Establish two project boundaries
cards.front: What should you record before a two-project exercise?
cards.back: The cluster/API, active identity and both exact namespace names so evidence can be attributed.

cards.topic: Build inside the cluster and identify the output
cards.front: What identifies a single build attempt compared with its reusable definition?
cards.back: A named Build identifies an execution. A BuildConfig supplies the repeatable strategy and output settings.

cards.topic: Build inside the cluster and identify the output
cards.front: What evidence shows an image actually reached the output stream?
cards.back: A successfully completed Build and a resolvable output ImageStreamTag digest.

cards.topic: Make the desired image serve real data
cards.front: Why can updated ConfigMap data and an old response both be correct?
cards.back: An environment-based setting is resolved at container creation. Replace the pod to load the new value.

cards.topic: Make the desired image serve real data
cards.front: What do ready EndpointSlices reveal and what else needs testing?
cards.back: They show eligible Service backends. A client must still verify response content and the intended access path.

cards.topic: Prove an image and a setting crossed the right boundary
cards.front: Where is access to a producer project's image granted?
cards.back: In the producer project, granting image pull permission to the specific consuming service account.

cards.topic: Prove an image and a setting crossed the right boundary
cards.front: Why can traffic stay healthy during a failed rolling update?
cards.back: Old ready replicas can continue serving while a new replica fails its readiness probe.

decks.title: Build from source and promote a verified digest

cards.topic: Build the reviewed Git revision
cards.front: Why record the resolved Git commit?
cards.back: A branch name moves. The resolved hash identifies the source the cluster fetched for that Build.

cards.topic: Build the reviewed Git revision
cards.front: What do the S2I assemble and run stages do here?
cards.back: Assemble prepares and checks the application source. Run starts the resulting HTTP service.

cards.topic: Package a reusable source-validation builder
cards.front: What is the role of the builder image's own digest?
cards.back: It identifies the toolchain artifact used to assemble the application, separately from the app's output digest.

cards.topic: Package a reusable source-validation builder
cards.front: How does the build log help diagnose a missing builder tool?
cards.back: First identify the builder that was pulled, then locate the invocation of the expected path during assemble.

cards.topic: Make a bad candidate fail before promotion
cards.front: What separates a webhook trigger from an image test?
cards.back: A webhook requests a new build. The postCommit hook executes a check against the resulting image before push.

cards.topic: Make a bad candidate fail before promotion
cards.front: What is the negative control for a rejected candidate build?
cards.back: The accepted digest remains equal to its archived baseline while the distinct failing Build reports its error.

cards.topic: Promote and roll back an image without rebuilding it
cards.front: What should select a rollback target?
cards.back: An independently recorded previous accepted digest, ideally accompanied by the expected version response.

cards.topic: Promote and roll back an image without rebuilding it
cards.front: Why might a successful oc tag fail to demonstrate a rollout?
cards.back: The destination may already point to that digest, or the workload may not watch the tag.

decks.title: Package independent releases with templates, Kustomize and Helm

cards.topic: Parameterize two cooperating containers
cards.front: How does NAME prevent two processed releases from interfering?
cards.back: It is applied consistently to resource names, selectors and configuration references.

cards.topic: Parameterize two cooperating containers
cards.front: Why observe paired through both its sidecar and its Service?
cards.back: The sidecar tests pod-local readiness, while the separate Service client verifies routing and business fields.

cards.topic: Use a Kustomize overlay without changing the base
cards.front: What change causes Kustomize-generated data to update a pod template?
cards.back: A changed config hash gives a new name, and Kustomize rewrites recognized references to that name.

cards.topic: Use a Kustomize overlay without changing the base
cards.front: What does rendering an overlay establish?
cards.back: It reveals desired resources and their cross-references. Server acceptance and live behavior require separate checks.

cards.topic: Use Helm to upgrade and reverse a customer release
cards.front: Why is a checksum placed on the pod template?
cards.back: Changing configuration alters the template hash and the Deployment creates replacement pods.

cards.topic: Use Helm to upgrade and reverse a customer release
cards.front: What happens to release history during Helm rollback?
cards.back: Helm records a new revision carrying the selected older desired state.

decks.title: Verify delivery with the registry, Tekton and an installed operator

cards.topic: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
cards.front: Why does a successful in-cluster pull say little about laptop access?
cards.back: Cluster service DNS and routes may not be available externally. The laptop needs its approved endpoint, trust and credentials.

cards.topic: Choose a supported access path to the internal registry
cards.front: What can a registry handoff safely include?
cards.back: The verified host, project, repository and digest, with login secrets excluded.

cards.topic: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
cards.front: How can you demonstrate that an acceptance pipeline detects defects?
cards.back: Run an intentionally wrong expectation against a known response, capture the failure, then run a corrected independent case.

cards.topic: Turn an acceptance claim into a Tekton run
cards.front: Which resource ties a Tekton result to a particular set of inputs?
cards.back: The PipelineRun names the pipeline and records the invocation's parameters, conditions and child runs.

cards.topic: Consume an installed operator through its API
cards.front: What does a served CRD establish?
cards.back: The API can accept the resource kind. Controller readiness and successful reconciliation need conditions and output evidence.

cards.topic: Consume an installed operator through its API
cards.front: What TLS evidence is enough for the namespaced operator exercise?
cards.back: A Ready Certificate and issuer, the Secret type and public certificate identity. Private keys stay in the Secret.

cards.topic: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
cards.front: Which records link code, artifact and customer response?
cards.back: The resolved Git SHA and Build, the verified image digest, the workload image and an independently read version.

cards.topic: Independent practical B — promote a reviewed application
cards.front: How do you show that a rollback stayed in its authorized project?
cards.back: Compare the rolled-back source image and response with baseline, then independently check the excluded project is unchanged.

references.title: Workstation, cluster and credential route
references.body:
## Start here

A learner should already be able to use Bash, Git, a text editor and basic HTTP requests. Start with the Podman stage if you can run a process but have not delivered an image. If you already maintain standalone containers, the workstation final gives you a diagnostic entry point before OpenShift. The second stage assumes project-scoped application permissions, the ability to read basic YAML, and familiarity with images and digests. The final goal is a reproducible application release across two projects with independent acceptance and rollback evidence.

Red Hat lists the developer credential EX188 followed by advanced developer EX288 for RHCE in Cloud-native Applications. Erudior provides independent preparation and original work orders. The current Red Hat pages name Podman 5, RHEL 10 and OpenShift 4.22 for the developer context and OpenShift 4.22 for the advanced exam. AlmaLinux 10 can serve as the Podman practice workstation. Exercises requiring OpenShift build, route, template and image APIs need an actual OpenShift cluster. Check your booked exam objectives by version.

## Prepare the environment

Use a disposable rootless Linux practice user with Podman 5, Bash, curl, Python 3, an available loopback port range 18080–18089, a trusted push-and-pull registry repository, and sufficient image storage. Some examples use 18081, 18084 or 18085; stop the corresponding port-forward before reusing it. Your account needs ordinary uid/gid mappings for rootless containers. Confirm access to docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim and registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311. Record immutable digests when preparing a reusable lab, since example base tags can move.

For stage two obtain oc compatible with OpenShift 4.22, Helm 3, Git, two assigned namespaces, a TLS-trusted API and ingress, working integrated registry, Builds and Routes. A source-project administrator provisions a narrowly scoped cross-project pull grant. Use OpenShift Pipelines with tekton.dev/v1 and namespaced cert-manager.io/v1 with a functioning controller. Acquire an approved Git remote reachable by the build service. A dedicated administrator may demonstrate the cluster-scoped registry route exercise. Cluster-provided quotas must permit a two-replica deployment and its sidecar. The exercises name their specific requirements. Secure any real tokens outside submissions.

## Saving a handoff

Keep revision IDs, object names, project, expected and observed outcomes, plus an explanation of the first failed boundary. The kit is sufficient to run the local HTTP application without external Python dependencies. Internet/registry or a preseeded mirror is required to obtain base images, and server admission, scheduling, operator reconciliation and registry authorization require the designated lab. Full practicals are reviewer-scored. Use the course's assignment links to record target observations.

references.title: Source comparison and further reading
references.body:
## Exam scope and skill comparisons

Checked November 23, 2026. The [Red Hat certification matrix](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/certifications?type=role) supplies credential sequencing. [EX188](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/training/ex188-red-hat-certified-specialist-containers-exam) defines standalone image and container operations. [EX288](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/training/ex288-red-hat-certified-openshift-application-developer-exam) gives the advanced developer scope, including builds, releases, OpenShift Pipelines and installed operators. Each original work order tests visible state independently of the certification exam.

[MIT subMIT’s Podman tutorial](https://submit06.mit.edu/submit-users-guide/tutorials/tutorial_3.html) works from a build recipe through local Podman execution and registry images. It then treats Singularity for research jobs. Here we keep the executable recipe and local run, then add rootless networking, image and data recovery, and a separate OpenShift application workflow. [UW–Madison CHTC’s container build guide](https://www.chtc.cs.wisc.edu/uw-research-computing/docker-build/) teaches build contexts, image distribution and testing an image for another execution environment. Its Docker/HTC commands are useful comparisons. This course exercises Podman on the standalone system and verifies OpenShift output against the same application contract.

## Product references

- [Podman create and runtime options](https://docs.podman.io/en/v5.6.0/markdown/podman-create.1.html) and [Podman save](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-save.1.html) for rootless runtime inputs and offline image archives.
- [OpenShift 4.22 builds](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.22/html-single/builds_using_buildconfig/index) for source strategies, webhook secret references, output and postCommit hooks. [S2I Python builder](https://github.com/sclorg/s2i-python-container) for the builder family used by the kit.
- [OpenShift 4.22 registry](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.22/html-single/registry/index) for approved internal and external access paths. [OpenShift images](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.22/html-single/images/index) for dependency tracking, cross-project pulls and image-change triggers.
- [Kustomize](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/kustomization/) for generated names and reference updates. [Helm templates](https://helm.sh/docs/v3/chart_template_guide/getting_started/) for values and release-scoped templates.
- [Tekton PipelineRun](https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/pipelineruns/) for invocation and status. [cert-manager self-signed issuer](https://cert-manager.io/docs/configuration/selfsigned/) for a namespaced exercise using an installed operator.

references.title: Choose an RHCE pathway
references.body:
## Choose a specialization

An operations team can put the same application in four different hands. The Linux administrator restores the host after a boot or storage failure. The automation engineer writes a play that brings many hosts back to the agreed state. The OpenShift administrator looks after the cluster and its tenants. The application developer builds the image, tests it and promotes the application. Choose the work you want to practice.

| Role and credential route | First stage | Engineer stage | Erudior practice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enterprise Linux | EX200, system administration | EX342, diagnostics and troubleshooting | Start with [Zero to RHCSA](https://app.erudior.com/rhcsa-rhel10-administration), then open [Enterprise Linux](https://app.erudior.com/rhce-enterprise-linux). |
| Ansible | EX200, system administration | EX294, advanced Ansible administration | Start with [Zero to RHCSA](https://app.erudior.com/rhcsa-rhel10-administration), then open [Ansible on AlmaLinux 10](https://app.erudior.com/rhce-in-ansible-on-almalinux-10). |
| OpenShift | EX280, cluster administration | EX380, advanced cluster administration | [OpenShift administration](https://app.erudior.com/rhce-openshift-administration) contains both stages. |
| Cloud-native applications | EX188, container development | EX288, advanced OpenShift application development | [Cloud-native applications](https://app.erudior.com/rhce-cloud-native-applications) contains both stages. |

The two Linux-based routes share EX200. An OpenShift application developer and an OpenShift cluster administrator use the same platform but prepare for different exam pairs. Each Erudior practical is an original learning exercise. Red Hat awards credentials through its own examinations.

As of November 23, 2026, Red Hat also lists the AI developer credential, EX267. Its public catalog lists no engineer-level exam for AI. Check [Red Hat’s certification requirements](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/certifications?type=role) for updates or a particular exam version before registering.

references.title: Evidence and scoring guide
references.body:
Knowledge checks use the built-in grader. Open an assignment in its lesson to submit target observations separately. The reviewer scores each rubric criterion as demonstrated (2), partial (1) or repeat required (0). To earn full points for a criterion, submit all its stated observable facts. Partial credit requires at least one relevant completed check with recorded target or run identity. If evidence is missing or contradicts the acceptance target, repeat that criterion.

For example, a ready Deployment establishes that the readiness criterion passed. It earns no independent credit for a particular returned audience unless the student also reads that response from the intended Service. A report containing no secret values is sufficient. Submitting an actual credential is never required. Record the reason access was unavailable rather than entering guessed cluster output. Finish that portion in an equipped lab before claiming it succeeded.

Accept equivalent implementations which meet the exact data, isolation and durability requirements. A screenshot alone without resource identity leaves provenance or namespace ambiguous. A failed run followed by a success is stronger evidence when it isolates just one changed input. The final capstones are original Erudior scenarios; local rubric points do not predict an official exam score.
